Thank you. We were together in Tenerife, actually, to fight hantavirus. him and Minister of Health Mónica were saying vamos, vamos very often, and I was wondering what's vamos, vamos, because everybody was worried about hantavirus, so they were saying move quickly. So for a second time yesterday, I heard vamos España, vamos. So we're colleagues fighting hantavirus, and I'm glad To see you here, special envoy Jean Todt and Michel Yao, Excellencies Ministers, Excellencies Ambassadors, heads of delegation, dear colleagues and friends. Welcome and thank you all for being here. Road deaths, as you know, are falling. Between 2011 and 2025, the global death rate fell by more than one-fifth. And yet, the decline is nowhere near fast enough to meet our goal of a 50% drop in deaths and serious injuries by 2030. At the midpoint in the Decade of Action for Road Safety, the time for talk is over. We must double down on delivery. Doubling down means moving from pilot projects to national policy, from good intentions to legislation that enforces it, and from short-term funding to sustained, predictable investment. We need bold national strategies with clear targets, timelines, and budgets. We need a paradigm shift towards making safety a priority. We must design streets for people, not motor vehicles. And we must promote a vision of mobility that protects people, prosperity and the planet. The Global Plan for the Decade of Action gives us the roadmap. It rests on 5 pillars, as we know. Safe roads and mobility, safer vehicles, safer road users, safer speeds, and better post-crash care. Progress on any one pillar helps, but real change comes when countries act on all 5 together. Speed remains one of the biggest determinants of whether a crash is survivable. Lower speed limits consistently enforced save lives in every country, at every income level. And the basics still matter most: seatbelts and child restraints, motorcycle helmets, and strict laws against drink and drug driving. Where these are enforced, deaths fall. Where they are not, progress stalls. Every government represented here has valuable lessons to share. Brazil, Ireland, Morocco, Spain, Thailand and the United Kingdom offer lessons in leadership and coordination. Brazil has shown what sustained political commitment and city-level action can achieve. Ireland has embedded road safety within its wider public health agenda. Morocco has strengthened enforcement and driver licensing. Spain has invested in safer urban design and lower city speed limits. Thailand continues to tackle the particular risks facing motorcyclists, who account for a large share of its road deaths. And the United Kingdom has built one of the world's most effective systems for road safety data and research. Each of you can learn from each other, and none of you should feel you must start from zero. This meeting is about sharing what works and why. WHO is proud to play a leading role for the UN on road safety. We help Member States build safe systems and strengthen strategies, policies, laws and regulations. We help translate evidence into national action plans. And we support legislative reform on the risk factors we know save lives. Speed drink driving, seat belts, child restraints, and helmets. We host the Global Road Safety Leaders Network, which supports national road safety agencies. We lead the creation of global guidelines like the Global Plan for the Decade of Action on Road Safety. And we track progress at all levels through regular Global Status Reports. Last year, there were over 1.1 million road deaths globally, more than 2 every minute. The burden falls heaviest on the young and on the poorest countries. Road traffic injuries remain among the leading causes of death for children and young people aged 5 to 29 worldwide, and more than 90% of road deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries. even though they have less than 60% of the world's vehicles. Every single one of those deaths is preventable, and none are acceptable. So today, I ask each of you to leave this room with one concrete commitment: a law you will pass, a budget you will secure, a street you will redesign, or a dataset you will publish. Small specific commitments multiplied across every country here are how we bend the curve before 2030. Before I close, I thank again Special Envoy Jean Todt for your leadership, and thank you all for your commitment to making the world's roads safer. Let's work together to turn pledges into progress. I thank you. And back to you, Étienne.

Thank you.

The latest estimates is that there's a 9% fall in the absolute number of deaths since 2010, which corresponds to a 21% reduction in the fatality rate because the population has increased quite a bit globally. since then, and 108 countries have reduced fatalities. It's worth stopping for a minute on these numbers, because when the car was invented 150 years ago and we somehow decided we were going to develop a car-based transportation system, as a result, the number of deaths started to rise, and it has risen almost nonstop for 150 years. With probably the exception of World War I, World War II, and COVID. So having, over a 15-year period, a 9% reduction in the number of deaths is a very major achievement of which we all collectively can be proud of, because that achievement would not have happened without concerted efforts. If we had not had concerted efforts, the number would have continued to rise and we'd probably be at 1.6, 1.7 million by now. So now we have started to see a decline. That's the good news. However, we still have 1 point— 1 point— yeah, 1.16 million deaths last year on the world's roads, which is a reduction the last estimates was 1.19, so this is indeed a reduction. So the leading cause of death for our children is not some kind of virus or some kind of bug that we cannot control. No, it's our own transportation systems that we have designed. So clearly, it's good to have a decrease, but it's very far from where we want to be. Next slide, please. Another way of looking at it is also in comparison to the number of cars and vehicles on the road. The green line is the mortality decreasing, as I said. The red line is the increase in vehicles on the world's roads. Since 2010, they've tripled. Well, thank you, Dr. Tran, and it's a great pleasure to be here this afternoon. We cannot afford to be complacent, and so the most important step that we've taken since many of us met in Marrakesh is to publish a new road safety strategy, the first in more than a decade, and it sets out a long-term target that's very clear. We want to reduce those killed or seriously injured on Great Britain's roads by 65% by 2035, 70% for children, and it's built around the Safe System approach. And I think really importantly, we're moving the conversation from aspiration to delivery through a programme of reforms across safer road users, safer vehicles, safer roads, effective enforcement. We're picking up those pillars as you rightly said, Dr Tedros, is that you can't pick one, you need to do it across the board. And we're also strengthening governance arrangements to ensure that there's accountability for delivery across government and across partner organisations. So I think in terms of what's made it possible, what remains the obstacle to faster progress, we've made that commitment as a government to taking that long-term approach to road safety. And we want to translate that ambition to delivery. So the first thing is about partnership. It's absolutely crucial to delivering our strategy. So that means working closely with all levels of government, so with our emerging, with regional mayors, with local authorities, clearly with the emergency services, the police as the body responsible for enforcement, and with non-governmental organisations to make it happen. Just reflecting on what has been said, and whilst it is, you know, certainly from an Irish perspective, welcome to be deemed best in class or one of the best in class, I can tell you from an Irish citizen's perspective that, and from a government perspective, that does not lead us to any complacency in that regard. Because when we talk about numbers with road deaths, and I fully understand why, and we've got to track numbers, behind every number is a person, behind every number is a family, is a community. And that's why I'm always at pains to say that when we're discussing raw numbers, and those raw numbers are people. and that— and the damage that has been done to that family, uh, and, and to their community, uh, is, you know, in many respects, life will never be the same for them. So I just make my remarks in, in that context. And whilst we obviously are pleased that we've made progress over a period of time in Ireland, the Irish citizen is, is still, um, impatient for more. And the government is is impatient for, for more measures, and we've got to balance allowing people go about their, their normal lives. Uh, you know, we— I might speak on, on micromobility as well at the moment, because, uh, Dr. Tedros asked me, well, what one new law would we bring forward? I might speak about that in, in a moment, because we've had 2 very recently. Is looking at the progress that we made, and yes, that's— when I look back at, again, numbers, and these numbers are people, and I go back to 1997, We had 472 road deaths in Ireland in 1997, and that reduced to 133 in 2021. But I would say that that has increased back up to about 190 in 2025. So even though the 3 deaths per 100,000 is something that we've, you know, that measures good progress that's been made, We see with the numbers that you've put forward of the increasing prevalence of motorised vehicles, growing population— thankfully in Ireland our population has grown by 1.5 million people since 1990. That might not seem like a lot for a lot of large countries, but that is like a big increase, and it's something that we've got to manage. So I suppose when I look at what we need to do, obviously better road infrastructure, which we're working on, but really importantly, as we mentioned before, about that cross- agency and local authority collaboration. So in the work that Donna does in the Road Safety Forum, for argument's sake, that informs policy, not just new policy, but implementation of existing policies, because what we all know is what actually, in many respects, what needs to be done in all of our countries, and there are unique attributes, like in Morocco, be that in Spain, be that in Brazil, there are different things we need to do. We've quite a dispersed rural population, we've big cities, but dispersed rural population where people depend on the car, the motorbike, those type of things. And sometimes in, in more rural areas as well, there isn't that level of enforcement or detection. So education is critically important too. So we've our Road Safety Authority, and that effectively has been a really significant change. And what, what it does, friends, is it brings everyone together. So not one ministry is— even though I'm responsible and I have a minister state specifically responsible for road safety. It's a cross-government effort, cross-agency effort to implement our overarching road safety strategy, and that's been critically important. If I look at, though, you know, how do we actually ensure that we change driver behaviour too? Because a lot of things relate to, yes, enforcement, better infrastructure, better public transport, which we're doing, but that responsibility as well for people when they get into a car or get onto a motorbike or an e-scooter, that they're— that they understand the, you know, the responsibility that they have too. And that's something that we've got to continue to work on through educational programs, which we fund to a very significant level in our schools too. But across the Road Safety Authority, one of their remits is education. You'll find when you go to Ireland— I was talking to Jean Todt briefly just before this, that every day, unfortunately, anytime there's a road fatality or road injury, I think this is— which is terrible— I think the thing is that's always reported on our national media. So it's to the front, forefront of the national psyche, and it's something that keeps me as Minister for Transport, you know, that it's always to the forefront of our minds, and that you will hear it on radio, you will see it on TV, and that that road deaths counter as well, you know, that statistic is regularly out there. So we've a big job of work to do. I think on infrastructure, I mentioned education, active travel is critically— I speak from an Irish context, but I've seen it across Europe. I had the pleasure of being in Brazil twice in the last year. I was in Morocco for one day actually earlier in the year, but I can see, you know, different countries, different populations go about their business. Schools are critically important. So we've brought forward a big program called Safer Routes to School, and effectively that is actually changing not just the infrastructure around it, but changing how parents and kids get to school. And when we were looking at in the urban areas in particular, a sizable percentage— and I'm not just going to pick it— a very significant percentage of people are traveling, bringing their kids to school under 2 kilometers, and they don't need to. And even though people might think it, it doesn't rain every day in Ireland either, okay? And then There's no such thing as bad weather, it's just you've got to be prepared for it, okay? So you've got to— so people can walk and cycle safely. But we've worked with schools on this, like things like we've— in my own hometown, we did a school streets program where we basically closed the street outside the school at drop-off and pickup time. And initially, that wasn't, you know, it wasn't actually welcomed, but it's changed habits and actually even on air quality with my other hat on as Minister for the Environment and Energy. Thank you. We actually now track the improvement in air quality, so reducing cars that are idling outside school, and kids actually enjoy walking and cycling to school and building that infrastructure. Initially, schools were a little bit sceptical about it, and now we're opening it up again later this year. We've over 470 schools participating in that. Again, in an Irish context, that's a significant number, and we're going to open it up again for more. So we pay for the infrastructure to improve that across the board. So there are things that work, okay? Then, as has been mentioned by His Excellency from Morocco as well, if you look at micromobility— and Dr. Tan, you mentioned it as well— we've a prevalence of e-scooter use, and for a lot of e-scooters being used particularly for younger people. And we have laws that anyone under 16 shouldn't be using an e-scooter, but people do. Actually, next week I'm bringing to cabinet to our government changes to the laws for registration, mandatory helmet usage on e-scooters and e-bikes, and also increasing the age to 18. Now, why are we doing that? Because about 50% of all pediatric head injuries that we're seeing now in my country are being caused by young— are not being caused by, but are happening whilst young people are using e-scooters, and that's something we can't ignore. We can't also ignore the fact that lots of people use e-scooters to go to and from work, particularly commuters, things like that, and they work. But we've got to always be watching change, and the one constant is change. So we've got to make sure that our laws and our regulations and our enforcement indeed keeps up to date, or in some instances gets ahead of where we think we're going to be. And that's why fora like this are so critically important. Our police and our enforcement services— and great to see colleagues here from Brazil— are critically important in that. And again, we've got to look at things like, which we're doing, about the right to pursuit, like how police force can pursue someone in a safe way, all those various different types of things. So the lived experience, both from advocates like Donna, from our police forces, our emergency services, we've always got to be listening.
Okay.

And so, look, I think myself that from an Irish perspective, we're obviously satisfied in the sense that we've seen a reduction in the deaths per 100,000 over that period of time, and we've actually implemented what the UN best practice is, and it's across government. Our road strategies are updated on a regular basis, but we can't allow— and I know no one here in this room— allow any complacency. Like, one road death is, is one death too many, and the vast, vast majority are preventable. So I think for us it's about listening. It's about listening to advocates like Donna. It's about listening to professionals like our enforcement, our police services, our emergency services who deal with these terrible instances. In conclusion, I was really struck a number of weeks ago— and sorry, Chair, for maybe taking up a little bit too much time. But there was, there was a young girl in Dublin who was walking across the street at a zebra crossing. Grace Lynch was her name. And a young man, actually, on an off-road bike, so a bike like a racing bike propelled, we call it a scrambler bike, actually went through and basically Grace died. and her, a 16-year-old, going about her business. And I've met her parents, and her parents, and you just see that their life has just changed forever. And like with Donna, and like with Grace's parents as well, they're using that terrible tragedy to bring about good, to try to ensure that no other young man or young woman actually dies in this incident. They're the things that that drive us in making the changes that we need to make. So, look, it's a real pleasure to be with you today and to thank the WHO indeed for convening this meeting, to know that you have our full support, and we're always learning. Every day is a school day too, so we've got to keep working on this on behalf of our citizens right the way across the globe. Thank you.

Thank you so much for that and for highlighting the importance of obviously listening, but also I think the importance of continuing to learn and to anticipate what's to come. I think that's a very key point in terms of thinking about how do we not only solve the problems of today, but think about how do we anticipate and prepare for the problems of tomorrow. And I love what you've done in terms of encouraging more walking and cycling, because from a health perspective, we obviously want to promote that as well, because it is actually not only better for the environment, it's better for people's health as well. I hope that more countries can learn from that experience. Finally, I'm going to turn to the Minister from Spain, and I'm not going to ask you how you managed to win a second World Cup. I am going to ask you about what you're doing and how you've managed to keep Spain safe from a road safety perspective. and how you've been able to do that, not just now, but over the last few decades?

Thank you. Thank you so much, Nan. First of all, I have to say that it's a pleasure, an honor for me to attend this meeting, so thank you so much, Tedros. Thank you so much, Nan, and thank you so much, the World Health Organization. I think that you are making a very nice work, a very great work. If you don't mind, I would like to answer the 2 questions at the same time. First of all, I have to say that winning the World Cup, it has been easier than road safety policies, I have to say. But we are working too hard. In the same line, I have to say. And for us, it's so important. It's one of the most important challenges that we face in Spain for a long time. I have to say that for the last 20 years, we have worked very hard on it. First of all, I would like to say that improving road safety is no longer a question of knowledge. We know the risk and we know the measures we have to put in order. In the last 20 years, as I told you in the beginning of my intervention, we have been working very hard. We have achieved, I have to say, significant progress through the implementation of a number of measures whose proven effectiveness I would like to put here. First, one of them: reducing the speed limit on single roadways from 100 to 90 kilometers per hour. For example, this is the, the safe system. We know that introducing a speed limit of 30 kilometers per hour on all urban streets with a single lane in each direction, for example. Establishing a points-based driving license system. I think that this one has been the most important measure we have put in order, whose effectiveness rests on a balance between enforcement and education. Risky behavior is penalized while ongoing education is promoted to strengthen respect for traffic rules. As the minister— Irish minister said before, incorporating road safety education throughout every stage of compulsory schooling. That is real here now in Spain. For example, strengthening support for victims of road traffic crashes through new assistance measures, including the creation of a national helpline for victims. These are some of the many initiatives undertaken in recent years. I would also like to emphasize that effective enforcement of traffic law is one of the most powerful means of reducing road traffic crashes and their devastating consequences. Monitoring, enforcement, and penalties remain essential pillars of road safety, of course. Education, of course, Self-protection, of course, but I have to say that enforcement and penalties is needed too. Talking about the governance, financing, accountability, how to manage road safety, how to improve, what do we have to do? I think that We have learned in Spain at this moment, and I think that we are learning each day, of course, we have learned 7 lessons how to act, how to manage. First, every transformation begins with political will. Some decisions, and we know all of us, are difficult, but when we know that a measure save lives, it's our responsibility to implement it. We are talking about implementation. Second, strong institutions are of course essential. Institutions capable of designing, implementing, and evaluating public policy. In Spain, we have a specialized National Road Safety Authority with clearly defined powers, technical expertise, sufficient resources, and consistent actions over time. Third, coordination. You have talked about that. Road safety involves many sectors and different levels of government. We work on an ongoing basis with other ministers— ministries, excuse me— as well as with regional and local authorities. In Brazil, 5,000 municipalities, more or less the same in Spain. That this cooperation, of course, among all of us is indispensable if policies are to be implemented effectively across the country. 4, evidence. And I think that that is very important for all kinds of policies, talking about science and evidence. The most difficult decisions can only be sustained by robust data. We use scientific evidence to guide our decisions assesses their outcomes, and make any necessary adjustment. 5th, building partnerships. You talk about it too. Reforms are stronger when they are developed in cooperation with associations representing victims, pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, drivers, road transport operators, driving schools, and vehicle manufacturers. 6, and this is fundamental, we must call on every citizen to take personal responsibility. Road safety requires awareness and a sense of shared responsibility. It concerns every one of us. Both collectively and individually, personally. Finally, seven, I think that it's very, very important. Sound policy also requires effective communications. Measures must be properly explained when citizens understand the. The purpose behind an initiative, public acceptance increases. I think that is quite important to explain all the measures we have to implement. We often ask ourselves, and today here, what needs to be done. Perhaps the time has come to devote more attention to discussing how we can make it happen. If we are able to share not only our policies but also our experience of turning them into reality, we will be closer to achieving— achieve the objective that has brought us together today: saving millions of lives on the world's roads. Thank you so much.

Thank you, Minister, for those very inspiring words, and I think that's going to be our new tagline: winning World Cup is easier than addressing road safety. Joking aside, I think what you've highlighted is that it's a very complex and nuanced topic, That it's not just about doing one thing, it's about doing many things, and it's about finding a right balance between education and enforcement. But also really what you're talking about is really bringing about a change in cultural norms, a shift in the way of thinking, and that is done through enforcement, but it's also done through education, and it's also done through communications and the engagement of media. And I think really that's what we've heard in different ways from the panel of other national representatives as well. But all of you, I think, have highlighted the importance of engaging with communities, victims' groups, and civil society actors who have a role to contribute in playing into contributing and informing, as you've said, listening to people. So with that, I'd like to turn to 2 colleagues, Donna, who you've already— who's already been mentioned, but also Sana, who represents And perhaps I can ask the two of you to reflect a bit on what has been said here from your perspective as victims, but also as youth and those that are going to shape the future of transport, of mobility, but also ensuring safety, to reflect a bit on what you've heard and what you think still needs to be done. So maybe I'll start with Donna and hand the floor to you to start your comments and reflect a bit on that.

Appreciate the opportunity to give the victim's perspective today, and I'd like to also thank my Minister for Transport from Ireland for including our NGO at home and for doing all in their power really to try and turn around the utter devastation that our families have experienced in losing a loved one on the roads or being seriously injured and being left really to pick up the pieces of shattered lives. As Jean mentioned earlier, we know the cure for these collisions. They're not accidents, and we all have a role to play really in preventing them. So in the International Road Victims Partnership, many of our NGOs have been founded by families whose lives have been devastated by road traffic collisions. Everything we advocate for is informed by the lived experience of victims and bereaved families, reminding us that behind every statistic is a person, a family, and a future forever changed. Our priority is to build a road safety system that both prevents tragedies and delivers support, accountability, and justice. Justice for those affected when tragedies occur. The greatest challenge now is ensuring that commitments are matched by delivery. Road safety strategies alone do not save lives. They must be translated into effective legislation, consistent enforcement, thorough investigation, and meaningful, meaningful support for those whose lives have been changed forever. That begins with robust legislation, including mandatory testing and other evidence-based safety measures, supported by effective deterrence and penalty— penalties that discourage dangerous behaviour. It requires rigorous enforcement because laws only save lives when they are consistently applied. It requires thorough investigations into every fatal and serious injury collision, together with effective prosecutions and appropriate sentencing that reflects the seriousness of the harm caused, so that lessons are learned, justice is delivered, and fair compensation is not unnecessarily delayed. It also requires timely information and data sharing compassionate support, and meaningful inclusion for victims and bereaved families throughout the criminal and civil justice process and during any public inquiries and coronial processes. Families should never be left traumatized by the very systems intended to support them. They should have timely access to information, justice, and fair compensation for loss and serious injury, together with the practical and emotional support they need to rebuild their lives. Finally, victims and bereaved families should not simply receive support after tragedy. They should be recognized as partners in improving road safety. Their lived experience helps identify system failures, strengthens accountability, and keeps our focus on preventing future harm. Every fatal or serious collision should leave behind more than grief and life-changing injury. It should leave behind knowledge, accountability, and action that prevents the next tragedy.
Thank you.

Thanks, Zana. It's always very inspiring to hear you talk, and we're so grateful for the passion that you and other colleagues here bring to this topic. And as a reminder that not only do you have an important role to play in sort of shaping the discourse and the conversations that we have, but also ensuring that the conversations don't end with the crash and with the fatality, and that there is a need for care and support and justice after the fact as well. So I want to thank you for reminding us of that. I'm going to invite our last speaker, Sana, who represents an NGO called Youth for Road Safety, to perhaps reflect a bit on what, what you make of all of this conversation. We often talk about youth being the group that's most impacted by road traffic crashes and road traffic fatalities. And I think it's also important to realize, as we heard this morning, by the way, from a very dynamic 16-year-old CEO, that youth also have a big and important role in shaping the solutions and how we think about the future of road safety. So, Sana, over to you.

Thank you very much, Dr. Nan, Dr. Tadros, Dr. Etienne, Mr. Todd, Your Excellencies. It's very important to have a voice like me in rooms like this. I do not only represent myself, yours, or even the Global Youth Coalition for Road Safety. I represent the biggest youth generation in history. So I want you to look at me but think of 1.8 billion young people around the world. Certainly, the world has changed a lot since the first decade of action for road safety, and I wasn't there, but Dr. Etienne was there, and we were fighting for road safety to be recognized as a political priority. But today, the situation is very different. We see road safety in public health, we see it in climate targets, we see it on the agenda of urban planning, digitalization, economic empowerment, and we believe that we've made a lot of progress. We are more ambitious than the results that we have seen on the screen, but young people can help accelerate this progress. And I would say that today we are at a much better place than we were in 2010. The core mission of organizations like yours is basically not to ask for young people to be visible in the room or to have a microphone in meetings like this. We want young people to have the power to challenge the system, to sit with decision-makers, to have more visibility on budgets, strategies, and to be able to influence. So the question is no longer, should we have youth in the room? Youth are already In the room. We want to challenge that and ask, what are we allowed to change when we enter those rooms? Do decision-makers have the political will to listen to young people and to reflect what they hear into the strategies and into all the decisions that will govern the future of our transport system? At the beginning, Mr. Todd has mentioned something about road safety being commitment, a mandated commitment for governments. He reflected that we need to have collaboration, we need to work together to reach those commitments. I want to add to that, that these commitments are not self-driving. We need active participation from the civil society, from the road users, from the community to directly deliver and design these commitments. Mr. Kayouh from the Ministry of Transport in Morocco mentioned the gap between the policies and between the processes that design the laws and design the regulatory frameworks that shape the system where people move, and between those— the people, the citizens, the recipients of those laws. And at Yours, we believe that young people can bridge this gap. Young people can act as catalysts and drivers to work closely with decision-makers to reflect the lived experiences of their peers on the roads into the strategies and the policies. Basically, this is one of the programs that we work at with yours and with our partners, who are— many of them are present in the room here today. We help governments learn how to work with young people. We design consultation mechanisms to help municipalities and city councils to take into account the lived experiences of those youth so we can prevent tragedies, the ones that are similar to what my colleague Donna has mentioned now. We can prevent this. And I believe that our biggest win has been achieved as yours. Young people today are not perceived as victims. We are perceived as changemakers, and we have been leading the work with governments in many cities around the world. And one concrete example that I can give you today is from our flagship program. It's called Local Actions, where we provide seed funding, mentorship, technical assistance to young people to design specific interventions in their communities. And basically, they receive like a very modest funding. It's around €5,000, but it is— it can be life-changing. One of our leaders in Peru, they took this funding and they developed a tool to basically collect data about unsafe cycling routes. So they started talking to their peers, mobilizing the community, and they came up with this map that allowed the government to know what are the dangerous zones in their cities. And with, with a very modest grant like this, they were able to attract $100,000 in funding, and now they are working closely with the city council to expand this tool and to replicate this experience across other cities, not only in Lima, but outside Lima as well, all around Peru. And this is a concrete example of what young people can do. Dr. Tadros, in his remarks at the beginning of this meeting, asked governments to leave this room with commitments, with more visibility for budgets, and also to work closely with civil society organizations. And I want to add to that, please include us in those decisions that you are taking. Young people, we are expanding our hands and we are— we want to shake your hand and to work closely with you to change the system. I share your optimism, Dr. Naan. At the beginning, you mentioned that we can achieve the target by 2030. But what I think about is that in 2030, sometime around that year, a child will go to school, and they will not be curious about the decisions that are made here. They will not be curious about the declarations or the targets. They will simply use that road, but that road will be decided by the decisions that are made in rooms like this. So we have the power today to change this, to make sure that we are preventing many unneeded crashes that could happen in the future. And I believe that we are— we can change the world if we can work closely together. Thank you very much.

Thanks, Anna. I think hearing you speak, I think all of us in the room become optimistic in terms of how we look at the future. I think you're also the first generation of young people or people that will look at road safety and look at a traffic death and say, this is not necessary, it's not a given. And I think that's really what's hopeful, gives us hope. And optimism as we think about how we move forward. Ladies and gentlemen, unfortunately, we are a bit behind schedule, so I'm going to skip the segment of questions and answers, and I would encourage you to approach the speakers here during the breaks for the next couple of days and continue the dialogues with them. So I'll hand it back over to Étienne for the closing.

Thanks.

Yeah, thanks, Nan, and I will skip closing remarks because we all need to move to the high-level meeting hall, but I just simply want to warmly thank all of our speakers. It was amazing to listen to all of you. I think if we put all of this advice, your 7 points and all of the others' experiences in a short document, it's a perfect guideline for ministers coming in having to deal with road safety. So a big thanks to all of you. I just want to give a shout out before we go to 4 road safety heroes. You're all road safety heroes here, those who have spoken, but I want to mention Rochelle Sobel, who lost her son 25 years ago and has never stopped fighting for road safety since then. I know she wanted to speak here today. There's no time, but I really want to mention her and thank her for all she does. And I want to mention Michelle. Michelle is an Oscar-winning superstar. She's been sitting here very quietly, but she's a fantastic road safety champion. So thanks, Michelle, for what you're doing. And I want to mention Benacer, Boula Joul, and Pere Navarro as examples of those who behind the scenes lead the work on road safety in their countries. They've been doing it for years and years. They are walking encyclopedias of road safety. They didn't say anything, but believe me, they're amazing champions. I was going to say Pere Navarro is the Amin Lamal of road safety, but both of you. So thanks very much. Let's move to the high-level meeting. Thank you all.
Thank you.
